newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU spurns military force, offers Tirana advisers.
newsitem.headline: EU spurns military force, offers Tirana advisers.

text.p: The European Union agreed on Sunday to send military and police advisers to Albania in a bid to help restore order in the anarchic Balkan state.
EU foreign ministers meeting informally in the central Dutch countryside also agreed to consider providing protection for this mission if necessary, but stressed this was not a military operation.
"Any interventionist approach is off the table," one German diplomatic source said. Sharp divisions over the questions of military intervention had emerged at the meeting on Saturday.

The EU said in a communique it was "strongly committed to helping Albania restore civilian structures and law and order", adding that outside help was needed immediately to restore security, in particular in and around Tirana.

"Among the member states there was readiness to send an advisory mission in the civilian as well as the police and military fields," it said, adding that it would first ask the United Nations whether it needed a mandate.
Officials said that they would consult the United Nations and seek its blessing for such a mission, although this would not necessarily be a formal requirement.

As a first step, the EU will send a high-level mission to Tirana on Monday, led by Dutch diplomat Jan Comte de Marchant et d'Ansembourg and including representatives from the Netherlands, Greece, Italy, the European Commission and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The EU statement called on Albania itself to take steps towards its own reconstruction. "There is a need for the Albanians to accept responsibility for rebuilding their country and society...to enable the EU to help them."
Ministers said they were ready to send humanitarian aid once it was safe enough to do so.
The 15-member bloc has struggled to forge a common approach on how to react to Albania's request for military intervention.

Stung by criticism of its indecision over the last Balkan conflict, in former Yugoslavia, several EU nations were keen to send a multinational peacekeeping force into Albania to try to prevent it from sinking deeper into chaos.
This was firmly opposed by Germany, Britain and Sweden.
"We can't get involved in another adventure," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said.
The EU statement made no mention of Albania's beleagured President Sali Berisha, whose ousting or resignation is seen by many as a first important step to diffusing the crisis.
Berisha has been blamed by many in the country for the collapse of pyramid investment schemes which bankrupted thousands and prompted widespread rebellion.

Some EU ministers made it clear publicly that they wanted Berisha to step down. Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo referred to him as a "stumbling block" when it was briefly rumoured on Saturday that Berisha had quit.
